v.q: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
o: Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you may do
Authentication decides what you may do; authorization proves who you are
They are two names for the same login step
Authentication is for services while authorization is for people
v.w: Authenticate first (identity), then authorize (permissions). Mixing them up is a classic interview slip.

v.q: Which statement about authentication and authorization is NOT true?
o: Authorization proves who the caller is
Authentication usually happens before authorization
Authorization decides what the caller may do
A role check is authorization
v.w: Proving identity is authentication. Authorization comes after it and decides permissions.

v.q: A logged-in user changes the id in `/accounts/1001` to `/accounts/1002` and sees someone else's account. Which flaw is this?
o: Broken object-level authorization (IDOR)
A weak password policy on the login form
Missing HTTPS on the account page
SQL injection in the account lookup query
v.w: The user was authenticated but the server never checked that account 1002 belongs to them. Check ownership on every object access.

v.q: An API returns an order to any logged-in user who knows its id. Which check is missing?
o: That the order belongs to the caller
That the password is long enough
That the page is served over HTTPS
That the id is a valid integer
v.w: The caller is authenticated but not authorized for this object. Ownership must be checked on every access.

v.q: Which HTTP status means "I don't know who you are"?
o: 401 Unauthorized
403 Forbidden
404 Not Found
409 Conflict
v.w: 401 means not authenticated (or bad credentials). 403 means authenticated but not allowed.

v.q: A caller sends a valid token but the account lacks the ADMIN role. Which status fits?
o: 403 Forbidden
401 Unauthorized
404 Not Found
200 OK
v.w: The server knows who the caller is, so 401 does not apply. 403 means known but not allowed.

v.q: Why are passwords stored with a slow, salted hash such as bcrypt or Argon2 rather than plain SHA-256?
o: A slow salted hash makes guessing expensive and hides repeated passwords
SHA-256 cannot be computed on an application server
Hashes can be decrypted later if the user forgets the password
A slow hash shortens the value stored in the database
v.w: Fast hashes let attackers test billions of guesses per second. A per-user salt defeats rainbow tables and a tunable work factor keeps cracking expensive.

v.q: Which statement about storing passwords is NOT true?
o: A fast hash such as SHA-256 is the best choice
A per-user salt defeats rainbow tables
bcrypt has a tunable work factor
Argon2 is designed to be slow and memory hard
v.w: Fast hashes let attackers test billions of guesses per second, so use a slow salted hash.

v.q: In RBAC, how are permissions granted?
o: Permissions are attached to roles and users are assigned roles
Each user is given individual permissions and nothing else
Permissions depend only on the IP address of the request
Roles are checked once at login and never again
v.w: RBAC groups permissions into roles such as TELLER or AUDITOR. ABAC goes further and decides using attributes such as amount, time or department.

v.q: A user holds the role TELLER. In RBAC, what grants them the ability to post a deposit?
o: A permission attached to the TELLER role
Their IP address matching the branch
A flag stored in the session cookie
The time of day of the request
v.w: RBAC attaches permissions to roles and gives users roles. Deciding by amount, time or department would be ABAC.

o: Proof from two or more categories: know, have, are
Two different passwords instead of one password
A longer session timeout after the first login
Encryption applied to the login page itself
v.w: Two passwords are still one factor. Combine knowledge (password), possession (phone or token) and inherence (biometric).

v.q: A login requires a password and then a one-time code from a phone app. What is the code?
o: Something the user has
Something the user knows
Something the user is
A second password
v.w: A code generated by a device proves possession. Password is knowledge and a fingerprint is inherence.

v.q: Where should authorization checks for an API be enforced?
o: On the server for every request, whatever the UI hides
Only in the front end, by hiding the buttons
Only once at login time, when the token is issued
Only in the gateway's routing table at deploy time
v.w: Anyone can call the API directly. Hiding a button is UX, not security. Enforce on the server, ideally close to the data.

v.q: Which authorization design is NOT safe?
o: Hide the delete button and skip the server check
Check permissions on the server for every request
Check ownership close to the data
Return 403 when a role is missing
v.w: Anyone can call the API directly, so hiding a button gives no protection.

v.q: A session cookie should be marked `HttpOnly`, `Secure` and `SameSite`. What does `HttpOnly` prevent?
o: JavaScript cannot read the cookie, limiting theft through XSS
The cookie is never sent over plain HTTP connections
Other sites cannot attach the cookie to cross-site requests
The browser deletes the cookie when the tab is closed
v.w: `Secure` limits it to HTTPS and `SameSite` reduces CSRF. `HttpOnly` hides it from `document.cookie`.

v.q: Which cookie attribute reduces the damage of CSRF by limiting cross-site sending?
o: SameSite
HttpOnly
Secure
Domain
v.w: SameSite stops the browser attaching the cookie to most cross-site requests. HttpOnly hides it from scripts and Secure limits it to HTTPS.
